A Convergent Subsequence Always Hides Inside

Every bounded sequence hides a convergent subsequence inside it. This scene finds that subsequence by halving the interval.

The trick is to keep halving the interval. Always follow the half that holds infinitely many terms. Each halving makes the interval narrower. The points trapped inside pile onto a single value. Stringing those points together gives a convergent subsequence.

For example, thirty 🧑 classmates scatter across a playground. Split the playground in half and one side still holds a crowd of them. Keep halving that side and you corner a single spot.

Find two convergent subsequences of an=(−1)na_n = (-1)^nan​=(−1)n and compute their limits.

a2k→1,a2k+1→−1a_{2k} \to 1, \qquad a_{2k+1} \to -1a2k​→1,a2k+1​→−1

  2. Taking odd indices, a2k+1=(−1)2k+1=−1a_{2k+1} = (-1)^{2k+1} = -1a2k+1​=(−1)2k+1=−1 for every kkk, so (a2k+1)(a_{2k+1})(a2k+1​) converges to −1-1−1.

  3. Both (2k)(2k)(2k) and (2k+1)(2k+1)(2k+1) are strictly increasing index sequences, so these are genuine subsequences. The bounded sequence (−1)n(-1)^n(−1)n was hiding more than one convergent subsequence, with different limits.

Show that (sin⁡n)(\sin n)(sinn) is bounded, and conclude via Bolzano–Weierstrass that a convergent subsequence exists.

∣sin⁡n∣≤1 ⟹ ∃ n1<n2<⋯: lim⁡k→∞sin⁡(nk)∈[−1,1]|\sin n| \leq 1 \ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\, n_1 < n_2 < \cdots:\ \lim_{k \to \infty} \sin(n_k) \in [-1,1]∣sinn∣≤1 ⟹ ∃n1​<n2​<⋯: k→∞lim​sin(nk​)∈[−1,1]
Show proof

  1. ∣sin⁡n∣≤1|\sin n| \leq 1∣sinn∣≤1 for every integer nnn, so (sin⁡n)(\sin n)(sinn) is a bounded sequence.

  2. By the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem, a convergent subsequence (sin⁡(nk))(\sin(n_k))(sin(nk​)) exists (its limit is some value in [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1]).

  3. The theorem only guarantees existence; it does not say which subsequence. As a numerical illustration (not a proof), terms pile up near 111: sin⁡(35489)≈0.9999990\sin(35489) \approx 0.9999990sin(35489)≈0.9999990 and sin⁡(36199)≈0.9999991\sin(36199) \approx 0.9999991sin(36199)≈0.9999991.

Prove that an=na_n = nan​=n has no convergent subsequence — showing why the boundedness hypothesis is essential.

nk≥k→∞n_k \geq k \to \inftynk​≥k→∞
Show proof

  1. Let (nk)(n_k)(nk​) be any subsequence of (n)(n)(n). Its indices are strictly increasing, so nk≥kn_k \geq knk​≥k by induction: n1≥1n_1 \geq 1n1​≥1, and nk+1>nk≥kn_{k+1} > n_k \geq knk+1​>nk​≥k gives nk+1≥k+1n_{k+1} \geq k+1nk+1​≥k+1.

  2. Hence nk≥k→∞n_k \geq k \to \inftynk​≥k→∞: every subsequence is unbounded above, hence divergent.

  3. A convergent sequence is bounded, so the unbounded (nk)(n_k)(nk​) cannot converge. Thus (n)(n)(n) has no convergent subsequence at all — dropping the boundedness hypothesis makes the theorem false.
